sections.title: The graveyard
sections.dir: Quiet and gripping, like the start of a true mystery. Pause after each item in the first paragraph. "So let's drain it." is said plainly, with a small pause before it. The last paragraph is warmer and direct.
paras: Off a lonely point on the shore of Lake Superior, there's a stretch of water that has taken at least two hundred and forty ships. A steamer that went down with seventy tons of silver ore. A freighter that exploded when the cold water reached her boilers. And seventeen miles out... the Edmund Fitzgerald.
Sailors call it the Graveyard of the Great Lakes. And almost everything it has taken is still down there.
So let's drain it.

We can't really, of course. But divers, sonar and two hundred years of shipwreck records have shown us what's down there. So we're going to lower the water, a few feet at a time, and watch the graveyard appear.
And at the very bottom, five hundred and thirty feet down, is the most famous wreck on the Great Lakes, and a question nobody has ever answered for certain.

This is Great Lakes Files. We go looking for the places hidden in and under these lakes. Our last Edmund Fitzgerald video brought a lot of new people here, so if that's you, welcome. sections.title: The door to Lake Superior
sections.dir: Steady and vivid, setting the scene quickly. Slow down for "Every ship entering or leaving the lake has to pass it." "Let's start the drain." is said plainly, with a small pause before it.
paras: The point is called Whitefish Point, at the eastern end of Lake Superior. Every ship entering or leaving the lake has to pass it.

Behind it lie a hundred and sixty miles of open water, so a storm from the northwest has room to build waves of thirty feet or more. Add fog, snow squalls, and a lane crowded with ships heading for the locks at the Soo, and more ships have been lost here than anywhere else on Lake Superior.
Let's start the drain.

sections.title: Twenty feet
sections.dir: Brisk and vivid, like a countdown. A short pause after each depth ("Twenty feet." "Thirty feet."). The last line drops lower, with suspense.
paras: Twenty feet. Just west of the lighthouse, which has stood on the point since eighteen forty-nine, the bottom starts to show, and the first wreck appears, in pieces. The schooner barge Saturn. In November, eighteen seventy-two, an arctic gale snapped the towline between her and the steamer pulling her. She was driven onto the bottom here and pounded apart. Seven men died.
A few miles further west, the same storm drove her sister barge, the Jupiter, ashore.

Thirty feet. Along the shore to the west, the wreck of the schooner Allegheny comes out of the water. She was stranded in a gale in nineteen thirteen. This time, the lifesaving crew from the station at Vermilion Point got every man off alive.
Not every crew here was that lucky.

sections.title: Fifty feet
sections.dir: Storytelling, building tension. Slow and steady through the rescue attempts. A real pause after "She sank in four minutes." and after "He was the only survivor." Respectful, never dramatic, for the paragraph about the crew.
paras: At fifty feet, a mile and a half from the point, the wreck of a wooden steamer appears. Her name is the Myron.

On the twenty-second of November, nineteen nineteen, she left Munising piled high with lumber, towing a barge called the Miztec. Two hours later, a November gale hit them, with winds of sixty miles an hour, heavy snow, and the temperature falling fast. The seas opened the seams of her old wooden hull. Ice built up on her until she could barely make headway.

Her captain left the barge at anchor to ride out the storm, and fought on toward the shelter of Whitefish Bay. A bigger steel steamer ran alongside to shield her from the waves. A lifesaving crew followed in a small boat.
A mile and a half from the point, the water reached her boiler fires. She sank in four minutes.

Her crew got into the lifeboats, but they were trapped in a sea of floating lumber. Two steamers tried to reach them. One got close enough to throw them lines, but their hands were too frozen to hold on.

Her captain was still inside the pilothouse when it tore away from the ship. He climbed out through the window and held on to the roof. Twenty hours later, a steamer coming up from the Soo found him, still on that roof, drifting miles away, his clothes frozen to his body. He was the only survivor.

Sailors say Lake Superior seldom gives up her dead. This time, she gave up every one. All seventeen men were found, still in their life jackets, covered in ice. Some were found days later, in a lifeboat. Eight weren't found until the next spring, frozen into the ice along the shore. Local people cut them free and buried them in a small cemetery called Mission Hill.

And the barge the Myron left at anchor, the Miztec? She rode out that storm. Two years later, she sank off the same shore with all seven of her crew. Today she lies a few miles from the Myron, at the same depth.

sections.title: A hundred feet
sections.dir: Calmer, with a sense of wonder. Read the last paragraph slowly, like describing a museum at night.
paras: A hundred feet. Seven miles out from the lighthouse, another wreck appears. The schooner barge Niagara. In September, eighteen eighty-seven, she broke loose from the steamer towing her and went down. All nine people on board were lost.

At a hundred and twenty feet, there's a steamer called the Vienna. She sank in eighteen seventy-three after a collision, and everyone aboard got off alive. In this graveyard, that makes her one of the lucky ones.

The water here is cold and clear, and wrecks last a long time in it. This is one of the last places in the Great Lakes where the wrecks aren't covered in zebra mussels. Three hundred and seventy-six square miles of it are now a protected preserve, and divers call it an underwater museum.

sections.title: Two hundred feet
sections.dir: Storytelling with a spark of treasure-hunt intrigue. Slow down for "seventy tons of silver ore from Montana." The last paragraph is direct and friendly, talking to the viewer.
paras: As the water falls toward two hundred feet, the wrecks get bigger. A steel freighter, the John B. Cowle, lies at about a hundred and eighty feet. In July, nineteen-oh-nine, she collided with another freighter right here in Whitefish Bay and sank. Fourteen of her twenty-four crew died.
And then, at two hundred feet, the wreck treasure hunters have talked about for a century and a half. The Comet.

On a clear, starlit night in August, eighteen seventy-five, she rounded the Whitefish Point light, heading for the Soo. Her lookout saw a steamer's lights ahead. Her captain turned, but it was too late. The Canadian steamer Manitoba struck her and cut deep into her side. A witness said her upper decks crumbled and sank in about a minute. Ten men died.

In her hold were five hundred tons of pig iron, some copper, and seventy tons of silver ore from Montana. People tried to salvage it in eighteen seventy-six, and again in nineteen thirty-eight. Both times, they couldn't even find the wreck. Divers finally found her in the nineteen seventies. But what happened to the silver ore is still unknown.

So here's a question for you before we go deeper. Where do you think the silver went? Still in the wreck? Scattered across the bottom when she broke apart? Or taken by someone who got there first? Put your guess in the comments right now, and if this graveyard is getting to you too, tap the like button. Then stay with me, because the deepest wrecks are still ahead.

sections.title: Two hundred and seventy feet
sections.dir: Serious and vivid. Read the explosion simply, without drama. A real pause after "Twenty-nine people died." and before "Twenty-nine." at the end.
paras: Below two hundred feet, the bottom of the bay falls away. And at the deepest point of the preserve, about two hundred and seventy feet down, lies the Superior City.
When she was launched in eighteen ninety-eight, she was the largest ship ever built on fresh water. The whole town of Lorain, Ohio, crowded the riverbank to watch.

On the night of the twentieth of August, nineteen twenty, she was heading down into Whitefish Bay with seven thousand six hundred tons of iron ore. Another freighter, the Willis L. King, was coming the other way. At ten past nine, the King hit her in the side.
Cold lake water rushed in and reached her boilers. They exploded, and her stern was nearly blown off. Most of the crew had run to the lifeboats, which hung right above the boilers.
Twenty-nine people died. Twenty-eight men and one woman. Only four survived. One of them was blown straight off the ship by the explosion, and was found floating on a hatch cover.
It was the worst collision in the history of Lake Superior. Remember that number... Twenty-nine.

sections.title: Five hundred and thirty feet
sections.dir: Slow, quiet and respectful. A real pause before "The Edmund Fitzgerald." Read the captain's words plainly. The last paragraph is calm and fair, like a careful reporter.
paras: Now the water keeps falling, past the preserve, past the mouth of the bay, and out into open Lake Superior, where the bottom drops away into the dark. Seventeen miles from Whitefish Point, just across the border in Canadian waters, five hundred and thirty feet down... she appears.
The Edmund Fitzgerald.

Seven hundred and twenty-nine feet long, the largest ship ever to sink on the Great Lakes. On the night of November the tenth, nineteen seventy-five, she was running for the shelter of Whitefish Bay through waves up to thirty-five feet high. She was about seventeen miles away. At full speed, that's just over an hour.

At ten past seven, her captain radioed, "We are holding our own." Minutes later, she was gone. No mayday. Twenty-nine men. The same number of lives the Superior City lost in these waters, fifty-five years earlier.

With the water gone, you'd see her lying in two pieces. Her bow stands upright in the mud. Her stern lies upside down, about a hundred and seventy feet away. Between them is a field of iron ore pellets, hatch covers and torn steel.

And here's something most people don't know. Her bell isn't down there anymore. In nineteen ninety-five, it was raised and brought to the museum at Whitefish Point. A replica was left in its place, engraved with the names of all twenty-nine men.

She's a grave. Under Ontario law, no one can dive on her without a license. And after more than fifty years, nobody knows for certain what sank her. The waves. The hatch covers. Or a hidden shoal on the way, like the one in our last Fitzgerald video.

sections.title: Let the water back
sections.dir: Gentle and reflective, slower. Pause between the things disappearing. The last paragraph is direct and friendly.
paras: Now let the water back in.

Lake Superior rises over the Fitzgerald first. Then the deep wrecks of the preserve. The Superior City disappears. Then the Comet, and whatever is left of her silver. The Cowle, the Vienna, the Niagara. The Myron and the Miztec slip under together. Then the Saturn's broken timbers, and the water is back at the foot of the lighthouse.

Tomorrow, freighters will pass Whitefish Point the way they have for more than a hundred and seventy years. Every one of them sails over this graveyard. And once you know the story, you never look at that water the same way again.

If you've sailed past Whitefish Point, worked on the boats, dived these wrecks, or visited the museum there, I'd really like to hear from you. One viewer of our last video sailed for U.S. Steel, and told us his crews stayed well clear of the shoals out there. Stories like that are the best part of this channel. Tell me yours in the comments.

And if you've watched all the way to here, you're exactly who this channel is made for. So if you haven't subscribed yet, do it now, and tap the bell. Because there are more graveyards hidden in these lakes, and we're going to find them. Thanks for watching.
